HEADLINE: Banks urged to keep cash flowing
TEXT:
Regulators have asked banks to ensure they can keep money in the system if the COVID-19 coronavirus forces branches to close as fears of the rapid spread of the outbreak wiped 10 per cent off the Australian sharemarket in a week.

As a growing number of companies banned overseas travel for Australian staff, the sharemarket plunged a further 3.3 per cent on Friday, sending it into official correction territory.

The horror five days has wiped out six months of gains and shredded $210 billion in value, making it the worst week on the ASX since the global financial crisis. The Australia dollar tumbled to its lowest point in 11 years.

On Friday, Prime Minister Scott Morrison conceded the economic impact of the outbreak would be the worst since the GFC, but insisted the underlying economy remained strong.

"There's a key difference. [The GFC] went to financial stability, financial markets, things of that nature. That's not what's at risk here," he said.

"What's at risk here is the breakdown of supply chains and the flow of people and goods and services because of the health issue."

Fears of a pandemic prompted panic selling on sharemarkets around the world, with the United States hit hard as the S&P 500 endured its quickest "correction" - a fall of 10 per cent - on record.

The US Federal Reserve is widely expected to move quickly to cut interest rates.

The Reserve Bank of Australia meets on Tuesday and. although a rate cut is considered unlikely, expectations rose on Friday as markets continued to dive.

New cases of COVID-19 were reported in Nigeria and New Zealand, and the outbreak has spread rapidly in South Korea. However, China reported its lowest number of new coronavirus cases in more than a month, although officials warned they did not expect the country's workplaces and schools to resume normal operations until at least April.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission chairman James Shipton warned that long-running hidden problems in financial markets could be exposed by the volatility "shocks", as he instigated a coronavirus "pandemic plan".

Officials from the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority have been communicating regularly with bank head offices to ensure crisis plans are in place to guarantee there is enough liquidity should Australia be caught up in an outbreak. APRA has also been working closely with other regulators.

"APRA has been in contact with regulated entities to assess whether they have adequate plans in place to deal with a possible pandemic," an APRA spokesman said.

Property giant Lendlease, Telstra, big banks including Commonwealth Bank of Australia and ANZ, insurance firm IAG and stockbroking group JP Morgan have banned staff from travelling overseas for work.

Telstra on Friday banned non-essential overseas travel until mid-March in an effort to protect employees from being infected. The ban extended a ban on travel to China implemented in early February.

The telco has also told staff returning from high-risk countries to "self-isolate" for two weeks when they return.

An Optus spokesman said the firm had "set up a daily emergency task force" and put in place contingency plans "to minimise service disruption and protect employees and customers". It has provided hand sanitisation facilities, masks and safety kits for staff working in public-facing jobs.

Japanese giant Asahi, which owns the Schweppes and Pepsi soft drinks business and a string of cider and beer brands, on Wednesday banned all staff travel to Japan and South Korea, extending an existing ban on China trips.

Sydney-based insurer IAG has had a ban on work travel to China, Hong Kong and Taiwan since mid-February. On Thursday morning, this was expanded to Japan, Italy, South Korea and Iran, a company spokeswoman said.

Westpac has had a plan in place for weeks, including no business travel to China.

"We are asking employees who have recently travelled to mainland China, or who may have come into contact with any people diagnosed with the virus, to work from home for a period of 14 days," a Westpac spokeswoman said.

An ANZ spokesman said the bank had "restricted travelling internationally to contain any potential spread of COVID-19. Any staff who have returned from China have been required to self-quarantine following advice from health authorities".

Vitamin group Swisse has advised its local workforce to temporarily cease any non-essential travel from Australia, and has asked staff in China to work from home and to "self-quarantine".

Aside from travel, local institutions are grappling with how the virus could affect their workplaces or supply chains should Australia begin to report more cases.

Supermarket giant Woolworths said its teams had "been encouraged to remain extra vigilant in following proper hygiene protocols in our stores".

As always, any unwell team member was being told to seek medical advice and "stay home until they have recovered", a spokesman said. It was also actively monitoring and responding to the latest public safety advice from health authorities.

Coles also said it was taking advice from medical authorities.

The supermarket giant had "comprehensive response plans in place across our network" but declined to give details about contingencies for stores.

It had been keeping in contact with suppliers - "not just those in China but also local suppliers who source raw materials or packaging from China", a spokeswoman said.

The spread of the virus initially hit Australian businesses such as travel agencies. But if it gradually chokes off supply chains, secondary impacts could arise on banks that have lent money to manufacturers reliant on goods coming from China.

Bank of Queensland also affirmed its own caution this week.

"We've started a review of our customer base, to see where we may have issues or we may need to provide more support for our customers," BoQ chief executive George Frazis said.

"Depending on how prolonged the situation is, I don't think we're going to see anything that's dramatic for BoQ given our mix of business. But . . . this is something we are watching closely."

WITH JAMES FERNYHOUGH, VESNA POLJAK AND PHILLIP COOREY

HEADLINE: In pandemic, home treatment likely
TEXT:
Specialised quarantine and hospital care may give way to home treatment for most Australians if they become infected with milder cases of the novel coronavirus, as the health system braces for pandemic conditions.

Infectious disease experts said the growing number of viral patients outside China, which led the Prime Minister to declare an effective pandemic on Thursday, meant that public health strategy would have to move beyond preventing an outbreak to slowing and managing it.

That involved at least two key priorities: ensuring proper diagnosis and treatment by managing the strain on the healthcare system, and reducing person-to-person transmission in the community.

Dominic Dwyer, a pathology network director at NSW Health and a professor at Sydney University, said the former objective would be achieved during a pandemic, in part by hospitals becoming tougher in their triage decisions.

"In a pandemic, hospitals become reserved for people who are very ill," he said, noting that home isolation for mild cases was a common prescription in the management of other diseases such as influenza.

The federal government's emergency response plan, issued on Thursday, refers to the encouragement of "voluntary quarantine of close contacts and suspected cases" if the situation worsens.

The World Health Organisation has not yet declared the coronavirus outbreak a pandemic, which it defines as the epidemic spread of disease in multiple locations.

Dr Dwyer said authorities would be carefully monitoring the preparedness of hospitals for a sudden surge in cases - especially the intensive-care units, emergency departments, and pathology labs - but that most had some spare capacity that they activated in the winter, when many viruses were especially active.

The fatality rate for the virus, which has killed 2858 people so far, is estimated to be around 2 per cent, and a major study by the Chinese Centre for Disease Control and Prevention found that 81 per cent of cases were mild.

Other strategies for managing the potential strain on the healthcare system included opening more beds, building spillover facilities, transporting patients to less populated centres, and deploying stockpiles of medicine and protective equipment.

ANU associate professor of medicine and infectious disease Sanjaya Senanayake said the effectiveness of hospital treatment might depend in part on the ability to adapt existing pharmaceuticals to treat the novel coronavirus.

Antivirals such as the Chloroquine, an anti-malaria medicine, and Lopinavir/ritonavir, an antiretroviral drug used to treat HIV/AIDS, were being tested for their potential application to the new viral strain.

"These are not approved or proven treatments but there are suggestions that they may help and, unlike a completely new drug, we know their safety profile," Dr Senanayake said.

On the second objective of reducing person-to-person transmission, health authorities could access tools ranging from public information campaigns to more direct actions such as forced quarantine and treatment.

Dr Dwyer said interventions that were closer to "nudging" people were preferable to more prescriptive approaches.

HEADLINE: Be calm, urges PM as budget damage looms
TEXT:
Fears over the economic impact of the coronavirus have intensified after global and domestic stocks were belted again on Friday and new government figures showed the budget was haemorrhaging badly even before the crisis struck.

Prime Minister Scott Morrison, who a day earlier put the country on pandemic alert, issued repeated calls for calm, urging people to go about their normal business and to keep consuming to stimulate the economy.

But as the ASX closed down a further 3.3 per cent on Friday, the prospects of the federal budget achieving its forecast surplus for this financial year became even more remote.

Department of Finance figures showed the budget bottom line for the 12 months to the end of January was $3.7 billion worse off than forecast just a month earlier when the mid-year budget update was released.

The economic impact of the coronavirus will start to show up after the January numbers.

Mr Morrison agreed that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak would be the worst since the global financial crisis of a decade ago.

"I think that's a fair assessment. The difference is this is not a financial crisis, this is a health crisis with significant financial impacts," he said.

"There's a key difference. [The GFC] went to financial stability, financial markets, things of that nature. That's not what's at risk here.

"What's at risk here is the breakdown of supply chains and the flow of people and goods and services because of the health issue."

The monthly financial statement for January showed the underlying cash balance for this financial year was a deficit of $26.6 billion - $3.7 billion, worse than what was forecast in the mid-year budget update.

Overall receipts were $4.8 billion lower than forecast with a large part of that - $1.7 billion - coming from lower than expected individual income tax collections. Surprisingly company tax estimates were in line with budget estimates of $53 billion.

If this trend continues, the government's forecast $5 billion surplus easily be could be wiped out.

Putting further pressure on the bottom line will be a promise by Mr Morrison to offer stimulus to the most severely affected sectors of the economy, such as tourism, exports, small business and education.

He said the stimulus would be "targeted, modest and scaleable" and sources said that "modest" was important. In other words, the government would not be spending billions.

"I don't think extreme fiscal responses are the right answer, and neither does Treasury," Mr Morrison said.

The Prime Minister said the measures would build on bushfire assistance initiatives such as in tourism. That sector was allocated to help promote tourism in the wake of the fires.

Mr Morrison blitzed the media on Friday to call for calm. He said Australia was well prepared and even if there was an outbreak here, the government did not envisage a lot of deaths.

"There's no need for (people) to take drastic or extreme measures or anything like that, they should go about their business.

"That's the best thing they can do also for the economy, they should continue to go out," he said.

There were no plans to shut schools, as had been done in Japan, or adopt any other such measures, Mr Morrison said.

Key pointsBudget bottom line for year to end-January is $3.7 billion worse than forecast.

Economic impact of the virus will start to show up after the January numbers.

HEADLINE: Chances rise for another slice to interest rates
TEXT:
The Reserve Bank is set to further downgrade economic growth on the back of coronavirus and collapsing sharemarkets, pushing the chances higher for another interest rate cut on Tuesday.

The central bank, which sent its entire China-based staff home before travel restrictions were enforced, has been monitoring the hit to supply chains and domestic consumption from the coronavirus.

Board members, who received their briefing packs on Thursday, will be weighing up the benefits of a plunging Australian dollar against concerns around a significant slowdown in exports and the increased likelihood of the Federal Reserve cutting its official interest rate.

Financial markets have raised the chances of a March Fed rate cut up to 90 per cent, while in Australia they rose to 18 per cent for March and 68 per cent in April.

Westpac's Bill Evans expects the Fed will cut in March but that the Reserve Bank will hold out until April. "Pricing for April has now reached a 60 per cent probability - a level of market pricing the board would see as reasonably consistent with a decision to move," he said.

Such a move would leave the bank one cut away from the point at which it would move to quantitative easing.

A poll of economists taken by Reuters showed the RBA would hold its cash rate at record lows next week and cut twice later in the year. As many as 29 of 35, or 83 per cent of those polled, forecast the first rate cut of the year to 0.5 per cent before June.

While an interest rate cut is unlikely to halt or reverse the worsening supply-chain mayhem caused by the virus, they could give businesses additional working capital to survive a temporary slump in demand or supply.

In early February the RBA said the coronavirus would hit economic growth by 0.2 per cent, but that is now likely to be revised higher when the central bank publishes its next forecasts. The four key areas the RBA is looking at are the top four exports - iron ore, coal, LNG and university education.

HEADLINE: Local holiday bargains the grim upside
TEXT:
As the Australian tourism sector braces for the full impact of coronavirus on the back of the devastating summer bushfires, at least there's never been a better time for locals to see their own backyard.

It's a grim silver lining for the industry. But the nation's 300,000 "mum's and dad's" tourism businesses - from B&Bs to kayak hire, and cafes - along with the big hotel chains and tour operators are beginning a period of near-certain prolonged discounting, with the full effects of coronavirus now tipped to run until June.

Over the past week, airline deals on offer have included Air New Zealand selling $69 trans-Tasman deals to stimulate softening demand, while Qantas was offering double the number of frequent-flyer status credits earned on bookings made as the airline tries to entice travellers back on the road, and reduce virus-related shortfalls.

Every one of the airline's domestic and international destinations will be on sale over the next month.

"Jetstar has a number of sales planned," Qantas also said of its budget-focused subsidiary.

Upmarket travel site Travel Associates (owned by Flight Centre) has strong offers "to support local", said Anna Burgdorf, general manager for brand and marketing - including the reduced price of $785 for two nights at Jackalope in Mornington Peninsula with a complimentary dinner thrown in and 20 per cent off the spa.

Travel Associates also has four nights at El Questro in Western Australia priced at $4089 - more than $1000 off the normal rate; while a huge range of deals offer variations on "stay three nights, pay for two".

"There's no doubt that local tourism needs our support after the recent bushfires, drought and flash flooding which has impacted the country, and with the addition of concerns around coronavirus, travelling 'at home' is a very compelling opportunity," said Ms Burgdorf.

Sydney and Melbourne hotel operators are offering discounts of up to 40 per cent as they scramble to fill empty hotel rooms due to the coronavirus travel ban amid fears it will soon be declared a global pandemic.

After a disappointing January for hoteliers and tour operators, with bookings down about 60 per cent, there were some "green shoots" appearing in February statistics, and Easter was tipped to be reasonably strong, said Simon Westaway, executive director of the Australian Tourism Industry Council (ATIC).

"The sense is, working Australians are getting on with their lives and are travelling but all the pointers are this will be closer to home," Mr Westaway said.

To push more Australians out to support one of the nation's biggest industries, the government is investing $20 million in an immediate new campaign through Tourism Australia - combined with about $20 million worth of investment from commercial partners.

Tourism Australia last week began the global roll-out of its new campaign, "There's Still Nothing Like Australia", which leans into its longstanding "There's Nothing Like Australia" platform. It comes on the back of the "Holiday Here This Year" promotion.

"Tourism is an incredibly resilient industry," said Phillipa Harrison, Tourism Australia's managing director.

"We have been through many crises over the years, and although we have a tough path ahead, I'm confident we will come out the other side stronger and better than ever."

HEADLINE: Events sector braces for cancellations
TEXT:
The boss of Australia's biggest convention centre says mass cancellations of conferences are almost inevitable as more multinationals issue blanket travel bans in light of the worsening coronavirus outbreak.

The Sydney International Convention Centre (ICC) has had only a "single digit" number of customers postpone or downgrade events since coronavirus hit the headlines in January, according to chief executive Geoff Donaghy.

One of those is Salesforce, the provider of customer relationship management software, which this month cancelled a regional user conference and converted it to a virtual event, but will still use the ICC's videoconferencing and webinar facilities.

However, even if the virus remained out of Australia, Mr Donaghy said the rising number of multinationals issuing no-travel advice to their workforce would have a "compounding and increasing effect" and that outright cancellations were probably inevitable.

Nestle, an employer of 291,000 people worldwide, grounded its workforce on Thursday, joining giants like Unilever, Apple and Goldman Sachs in banning or limiting travel.

ICC has several international events scheduled for its 35,000 square metres of exhibition space in the coming weeks, including global symposiums on smart cities and endoscopy in March. It will take the Australian Government's Department Of Health declaring a coronavirus pandemic to trigger force majeure provisions in ICC contracts with its customers, which would allow them to cancel events and be refunded any holding deposits.

However, Mr Donaghy said it was already working with clients to postpone or downgrade events, with those that had expected a large proportion of delegates to travel from or through Asia being most affected so far.

The ICC was already rolling over holding deposits until events could be rescheduled - even where strict contractual terms might allow it to retain the funds - in the interests of its repeat customers and Australia's reputation.

In the meantime Mr Donaghy said all of the venues owned by ICC's parent company, ASM Global, had moved to heightened hygiene standards, including hand sanitiser facilities at all entries and exits, and "far more regular" disinfecting and wiping all internal surfaces.

HEADLINE: Fund tanks as ASIC pushes fee ban
TEXT:
Investors in global investment giant KKR's listed debt fund have lost almost 10 per cent of their capital, as corporate cop James Shipton declared he wants the government to scrap stockbroker commissions for selling these types of complex financial products.

KKR raised $925 million in November for a new high-yield listed investment trust from retail investors who paid an issue price of $2.50 and who will also pay KKR ongoing investment management fees of about 1.58 per cent annually.

Treasurer Josh Frydenberg in January set up a snap review to consider closing a loophole that allows brokers and advisers to receive commissions, often between 1 and 3 per cent but sometimes higher, for selling new listed investment companies (LICs) and listed investment trusts (LITs), including real estate investment trusts (REITs).

It follows revelations by The Australian Financial Review that the corporate regulator secretly warned Treasury that dozens of listed investment funds that have raised tens of billions of dollars from retail investors are rife with "poor performance" and are paying "conflicted" commissions to financial advisers for "worse" returns.

KKR paid stockbrokers and advisers total selling fees of more than $20 million to float the leveraged debt LIT on the Australian Securities Exchange.

KKR's fund was the ASX's biggest ever debt LIT listing. Many retail investors were looking for a safe fixed income product to put their cash to outperform low-return bank term deposits.

Since its November 22 listing, the KKR debt LIT price has tanked to as low as $2.27 on Friday, more than 10 per cent below its last reported net tangible asset (NTA) value of $2.53 at the end of January.

Its share price traded at an intraday low of 9.2 per cent below the float price.

The KKR debt LIT has declined in value because of the stress in global junk bond markets.

Mr Shipton, chairman of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, said the regulator had been consistent for a "long time" in advising the government that the problematic "conflicted remuneration" model for LICs and LITs should be banned.

"Listed investment trusts and listed investment companies should not benefit from the carve out on stamping fees," he told a parliamentary hearing in Canberra on Friday.

"We have been aware of concerns in the market for quite some time."

Mr Shipton said the Hayne royal commission had exposed that conflicted remuneration, such as stamping fees, showed that the "self interest" of brokers and advisers will "trump" their "best interests duty" obligation to clients.

"We are also concerned about the potential, if not real, distortions in allocation of assets that can come from conflicted remuneration," Mr Shipton said.

An LIC or LIT is an ASX-listed company or trust set up to invest in a portfolio of securities managed by a fund manager.

HEADLINE: Follow the money
TEXT:
■ Sports rorts: A scathing audit of the $100m community sports fund sparked Bridget McKenzie's resignation, throwing the Coalition into damage control. Hearings revealed Sport Australia warned about the risk of politicisation and communities are angry at missing out. An inquiry into the grants has been extended to June.

■ Regional rorts: In November, the Auditor-General blasted management of the $220 million Regional Jobs and Investment Packages. No records were kept as ministers overturned departmental advice, including on a $5 million grant to a meat processing business linked to a Coalition donor. About 17 per cent of spending went to projects not recommended.

Labor will use Senate estimates to investigate this further.

■ Roads rorts: Analysis of the $3 billion Urban Congestion Fund suggests 83 per cent of funds have gone to Coalition and marginal seats. Labor's Catherine King says 28 per cent of the funds have been spent in four Liberal seats. The Auditor-General has been asked to investigate.

■ Pool rorts: The North Sydney Olympic Pool received $10 million from the so-called Female Facilities and Water Safety Stream. The $150 million fund was meant to go to regional projects. Labor calls it "a massive slap in the face" to Australians in rural and regional areas.

TOM McILROY

HEADLINE: Senior official destroyed notes on sports grants
TEXT:
A senior public servant has revealed she destroyed personal notebooks detailing talks about the Morrison government's sports rorts saga, a day before her retirement.

Outgoing Health Department secretary Glenys Beauchamp - who retires from the department on Friday - has told Parliament she has no record of late-night talks hastily convened after officials learnt then minister Bridget McKenzie was using a colour-coded spreadsheet to award $100 million in controversial sports grants.

Ms Beauchamp was part of the conference call, with former Sport Australia boss Kate Palmer and board chair John Wylie, organised after Ms Palmer was shown a spreadsheet highlighting Coalition-targeted marginal seats in the pre-election grant round.

The veteran public servant said she had destroyed all her notebooks and other personal records as she prepared to retire last month.

She was asked to stay on while her appointed successor, chief medical officer Brendan Murphy, manages the government's coronavirus response.

The extent of any notes she kept about the sports grants talks are not known. Public servants are not required to keep all records, and Labor has asked for clarity from the Public Service Commission.

Ms Beauchamp said the notebooks contained only her own "scratchings" on a range of issues, and she had a practice to "translate" notes into other official records including emails.

"As a private citizen, I should not have notebooks and things after midnight tonight," she told an inquiry into the Coalition's sports rorts saga.

Earlier, Ms Palmer told MPs she was "surprised" the colour-coded spreadsheet existed. It replaced Sport Australia's assessment of community projects. "I can't recall what it looked like. I was just surprised when I saw it," she said.

The issue was referred to Sport Australia's finance and risk committee, around the time the Auditor-General began an independent review.

Prime Minister Scott Morrison has rejected evidence from the inquiry, denying approvals were made after the start of the pre-election caretaker period.

Senator McKenzie sent a revised approvals list to officials at 8.46am on April 11 last year, the day the federal election was called. Labor argues that is a breach of caretaker conventions because Parliament had been dissolved for the poll at 8.29 that morning.

Mr Morrison said it was "not true" approvals were sent after the caretaker period began. "It was signed on April 4, 2019, that was the authorisation of the brief that went on that matter. The suggestion that it was signed at some time later, well there's no basis for that."

HEADLINE: Investor loans on rise again
TEXT:
Lending to investors for housing grew in January for the first time since December 2018 as record low interest rates and higher house prices drove buyers into the market.

Lending for business also recorded its strongest monthly growth since March last year, at 0.5 per cent.

The credit figures compiled by the Reserve Bank of Australia hint at what the central bank identified as a gentle turning point in the economy before the hits from bushfires and coronavirus.

Total credit grew by 0.3 per cent in January, above expectations of a 0.2 per cent and lifting annual growth to 2.5 per cent from 2.4 per cent.

Lending to property investors grew 0.1 per cent in January, but was still down 0.3 per cent for the year. Lending to owner-occupiers grew 0.4 per cent in January and was up 5.1 per cent over the year.

House prices across Australia's capital cities rose solidly during January, albeit at a slower pace than the previous month.

In the three months to the beginning of January, home values surged 4 per cent - the fastest quarterly growth in a decade - which may have attracted some investors back into the market.
